title: Raphael Shefer: A David-Horodok Zionist’s work of escape and rescue
summary: Shefer’s path from local Zionist activism to refugee-rescue work connects David-Horodok to a wider story of wartime aid.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Rafael Shefer reached the Land of Israel

editorialContent:

## A hometown beginning

The memorial book remembers Raphael Shefer—also rendered Rafael Shafer—as a son of David-Horodok who carried the town’s Zionist commitments into wider public work. Its account says he was born there in 1892 and began his Zionist activity as a teacher in the district school. His story is preserved in a memorial-book profile, [Raphael Shefer](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_b95b556973f3279112b512e2), and in separate records of his wartime movements: [his journey to Vilna](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_11b7548ab2f646b3ce4c6f42) and [his arrival in the Land of Israel](/communities/david-horodok/records/event_candidate_00e774ce7eb1e9f956472504).

The memorial account portrays Shefer not as a combatant, but as an organizer whose work depended on administration, information, and practical arrangements for migration. After the First World War, he moved to Warsaw. In 1921, according to the book, he joined the [Central Palestine Office in Warsaw](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_7739143a0f12840f998f93ce), first directing its information division and helping organize large-scale aliyah from Poland via Romania. In 1925 he became director. The book says he continued in that role through the outbreak of the Second World War and into the Nazi occupation, until conditions left no remaining possibility of arranging aliyah.

The profile also brings a personal voice to his public career. It describes Shefer as quiet and gentle, someone who confided his pain to friends rather than confronting problems forcefully. This is one memorial writer’s portrait, not an independent assessment. Yet it sits alongside the account of a demanding public role: organizing travel and assisting groups of emigrants amid increasingly restrictive conditions.

## From Warsaw to Vilna

The memorial book says that in 1940 Shefer left for [Vilna](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_bc08ebcfaa79ca865df305cc) with a group of Zionist activists. It does not provide a precise day, route, or account of the group’s composition. The date matters because Vilna was then a temporary refuge for Jews fleeing war and occupation. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum describes Polish Jewish refugees gathering in Lithuania in 1939–40, including Zionist youth and politically active refugees, while aid organizations helped provide food, housing, and other support. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/polish-jewish-refugees-in-lithuania-1939-40?utm_source=openai))

The wider record thus helps locate Shefer’s movement without confirming the details of his own journey. Vilna’s importance arose from its position between the German and Soviet zones of occupied Poland and the changing political status of Lithuania. Refugees who reached the city faced uncertainty, precarious legal status, and narrowing options for onward travel. The museum’s account describes how Soviet occupation in 1940 made politically active refugees especially vulnerable and intensified the urgency of finding routes out. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/polish-jewish-refugees-in-lithuania-1939-40?utm_source=openai))

For David-Horodok, Shefer’s departure represented a striking extension of local experience: a man who had begun as a teacher in the town became a professional organizer in Warsaw, then joined fellow activists amid a continental refugee crisis. The memorial book does not name the other members of the Zionist group or tell us whether they all followed the same route afterward. That absence should remain visible rather than be filled in by assumption.

## Tehran and the work of rescue

The supplied memorial-book records connect Shefer with the [Jewish Agency](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_118615b8ab8c3232ec117cf3) and say he went to [Tehran](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_3d3f7b6455041ea0b6a09970) to organize aliyah for Polish refugees arriving from the Soviet Union through Persia. A further record states that he continued this work with the [Rescue Committee](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_2ee871f4ae7efa862162efb7) after returning from Tehran. These traces show an organizer moving between institutions and places; they do not spell out the precise dates of his Tehran service, the number of people he assisted, or the individual journeys he arranged.

The independent historical record establishes the scale and context of refugee movement through Iran, not Shefer’s personal role. The USHMM reports that Polish civilians and soldiers reached Iran from the Soviet Union in 1942, including Jewish children who had been separated from their families or orphaned. Some of the children were eventually admitted to Palestine after negotiations involving Zionist leaders, Polish officials, and British authorities. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/tehran-children?utm_source=openai)) The museum’s broader account of Polish refugees in Iran describes the difficult arrival, quarantine, and dispersal of refugees after reaching the country. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/polish-refugees-in-iran-during-world-war-ii?utm_source=openai))

These sources make the memorial book’s brief reference to Tehran legible as part of a complex rescue effort involving transit, relief, and immigration permissions. But they do not independently name Shefer as an organizer in Iran. His role is therefore known here through the David-Horodok memorial book, while the wider record illuminates the refugee emergency in which that work took place.

The book also says Shefer ultimately reached the [Land of Israel](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_be96698fcf1de80a850bb54f) with a [group of Zionist leaders](/communities/david-horodok/records/mention_9c2686e0a083142e7e548a49). The account does not give a date or identify everyone traveling with him. Nor should this arrival be confused automatically with any one of the specific refugee transports documented by USHMM: the memorial record does not say Shefer traveled on those children’s routes.

## What the record preserves—and leaves open

The memorial account places Shefer in the orbit of Yitzhak Gruenbaum, identified in the records as a mentor and a Zionist leader. It also traces his work from the Warsaw office to wartime refugee rescue and eventual arrival in the Land of Israel. But the surviving material presented here is concise. It names no spouse, children, or other close relatives, and it does not establish their fates. A necrology listing “Shafer, Rafael” among David-Horodok natives who died in the Land is another memorial-book trace, but by itself it supplies no family relationships or further biography.

The variants—Raphael Shefer, Rafael Shafer—are consistent with transliteration differences, but the record does not explain them. Likewise, the connection between Shefer’s move to Vilna in 1940 and his later Tehran work is clear in the broad outline, not in every intervening step. These gaps do not diminish the account; they mark where further research could add names, dates, and documentary detail.

For David-Horodok, Shefer’s remembered significance lies in turning a town-bred Zionist commitment into organized action across borders. The memorial book preserves the trajectory and the community’s sense of his service. Independent histories explain the perilous refugee settings around Vilna and Tehran. Read together, they show both the reach of one David-Horodok native’s work and the limits of what can responsibly be claimed about it.
